newsitem.title: FRANCE: BAe eyes future European aerospace group.
newsitem.headline: BAe eyes future European aerospace group.

text.p: A senior British Aerospace Plc (BAe) executive reiterated on Tuesday a call for a giant pan- European aerospace company and outlined the firm's vision of what the group could look like.

The future single company would be made up of the merged French companies Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation, BAe and Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG of Germany, BAe group managing director John Weston told a business conference here.
The core businesses of the new entity would be civil and military aviation, weapons systems and systems integration.

The present national companies would be dissolved and reconstituted into the new group, which would have a dispersed shareholder base of private investors, who would exchange their current holdings for stock in the new company.

There would be guarantees that no single company or group of companies acting in concert could control the company and stakes could be capped at between eight to 13 percent of the capital, Weston suggested.
The parities for exchange would have to be agreed and be based on valuations.
The Airbus Industrie consortium would be part of the new group, but would be dedicated to civil aircraft, which provides the main growth market.
Governments could retain a "golden share" to protect vital national interests, or for use in emergencies.

The company would have a single unified management structure, but retain national head offices in each of the three countries to be the contact point with government, handle compliance and export rules and also give a national identity for the group.
Manufacturing and "centres of excellence" would be shared out among the countries, but on a rationalised and equitable basis.
A "Big Bang" transformation was desirable, but if it were not possible, then an intermediate holding company could be formed as a temporary step, even though this would create other problems.
Such a company would need "active political support" and break with the present defence culture.

But if Europe did not consolidate quickly, it would be reduced to a niche player with a narrow technological base, confronted with a U.S. industry that will be reaping the benefits of restructuring, Weston said.
